Summary

Minerals and trace elements are inorganic micronutrients required for enzymatic reactions, oxygen transport, antioxidant defense, connective tissue integrity, and thyroid hormone synthesis. Board-relevant topics include iron deficiency and hereditary hemochromatosis, copper disorders such as Menkes and Wilson disease, iodine physiology and thyroid hormone synthesis, selenium deficiency with Keshan disease, zinc deficiency with acrodermatitis enteropathica, fluoride effects on enamel, and the catalytic roles of manganese and molybdenum in the urea cycle and purine catabolism, respectively.

Iron

Biochemistry & Metabolism

Dietary iron exists in two forms:

Heme iron: Fe2+, found in animal products, absorbed directly via heme carrier protein 1

Non-heme iron: Fe3+, plant-derived, must be reduced to Fe2+ by duodenal cytochrome B before absorption via divalent metal transporter 1 (DMT-1)

Absorbed iron enters the portal circulation bound to transferrin and is stored in hepatocytes and macrophages as ferritin or hemosiderin

Systemic iron homeostasis is regulated by hepcidin, a hepatic peptide that inhibits ferroportin (the iron exporter on enterocytes and macrophages), reducing intestinal iron absorption and iron release from stores when levels are adequate

Vitamin C enhances non-heme iron absorption by maintaining iron in the Fe2+ state

Phytates, tannins, and calcium inhibit absorption

Deficiency (Iron Deficiency Anemia)

Iron deficiency is the most common nutritional deficiency worldwide.

Etiology

Chronic blood loss (GI bleeding, menorrhagia)

Inadequate intake (eg, strict vegan diet, malnutrition)

Malabsorption (eg, celiac disease, achlorhydria, post-gastrectomy)

Increased demand (eg, pregnancy, infancy)

Clinical presentation

Fatigue

Pallor

Tachycardia

Koilonychia (spoon-shaped nails)

Glossitis

Angular cheilosis

Pica (craving non-food items)

Dysphagia combined with pharyngeal webs (Plummer-Vinson syndrome)

Laboratory findings

Microcytic, hypochromic anemia

Low mean corpuscular volume

Elevated red cell distribution width

Treatment

Oral ferrous sulfate is first-line

IV iron is used when oral therapy fails or is poorly tolerated (eg, inflammatory bowel disease, post-bariatric surgery)

Reticulocytosis peaks at 7-10 days after initiating therapy

Toxicity/Excess

Hereditary Hemochromatosis

Epidemiology: most common inherited metabolic disorder in people of Northern European descent

Etiology: most cases involve a homozygous C282Y mutation in the HFE gene (chromosome 6). HFE protein normally interacts with transferrin receptor to sense iron saturation; loss of function leads to inappropriately low hepcidin production and excess iron absorption

Pathophysiology: dysregulated iron absorption, leading to progressive iron deposition in liver, pancreas, heart, skin, pituitary, and joints

Classic triad

Bronze diabetes (skin hyperpigmentation + diabetes mellitus)

Cirrhosis

Cardiomyopathy

Additional features include hypogonadism, arthropathy (especially second and third metacarpophalangeal [MCP] joints), and elevated liver enzymes

Screening

Transferrin saturation > 45% is the most sensitive initial test

Elevated serum ferritin is supportive but nonspecific

Confirmatory testing uses HFE genetic testing for C282Y homozygosity

Treatment

Therapeutic phlebotomy (removing 1 unit of blood per week until ferritin < 50 ng/mL, then maintenance phlebotomy)

Chelation with deferoxamine is used when phlebotomy is contraindicated (eg, significant anemia)

Complications: hepatocellular carcinoma risk is increased ~200-fold in patients with hereditary hemochromatosis and cirrhosis. Phlebotomy reduces but does not eliminate this risk

Lab findings: the table below summarizes the pattern of iron studies in deficiency vs. overload

Zinc

Biochemistry & Function

Zinc is required for the activity of more than 300 enzymes, including carbonic anhydrase, alkaline phosphatase, carboxypeptidase, and RNA/DNA polymerases

Zinc also serves a structural role in zinc-finger transcription factors and nuclear hormone receptors

Absorbed in the small intestine via ZIP4 transporter (encoded by SLC39A4)

Deficiency

Zinc deficiency is most dramatically illustrated by acrodermatitis enteropathica

Etiology: autosomal recessive disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in SLC39A4 (ZIP4 transporter), impairing intestinal zinc absorption

Classic triad: perioral and perineal dermatitis, diarrhea, and alopecia

Onset typically occurs when an infant is weaned from breast milk, which contains a zinc-specific binding protein (picolinic acid) that enhances absorption

Acquired zinc deficiency

Occurs with poor dietary intake, total parenteral nutrition without supplementation, malabsorption (eg, Crohn disease), or alcohol use disorder

Impaired wound healing, dysgeusia and dysosmia (altered taste and smell), immune dysfunction (particularly T-cell-mediated), hypogonadism, and delayed puberty

Treatment: oral zinc supplementation

Toxicity

Excess zinc supplementation inhibits copper absorption in the intestine

Induces metallothionein, which preferentially binds copper and prevents its transfer into the bloodstream

Chronic zinc excess can thus cause a secondary copper deficiency, presenting with microcytic anemia and neurological dysfunction

This is a high-yield mechanism: zinc is sometimes used therapeutically in Wilson disease specifically to reduce copper absorption.

Copper

Biochemistry & Function

Copper serves as a redox-active cofactor in several critical enzymes:

Ceruloplasmin (ferroxidase activity): oxidizes Fe2+ → Fe3+ for loading onto transferrin; also an acute-phase protein

Cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV of the electron transport chain)

Dopamine β-hydroxylase (dopamine → norepinephrine)

Lysyl oxidase (crosslinks collagen and elastin; connective tissue integrity)

Superoxide dismutase 1 (SOD1) (antioxidant defense)

Copper is absorbed in the small intestine and transported to the liver, where it is incorporated into ceruloplasmin and exported to tissues or excreted in bile via ATP7B.

Deficiency (Menkes Disease)

X-linked recessive disorder caused by mutations in ATP7A, encoding a copper-transporting ATPase expressed in intestinal and placental cells

Loss of function of the copper-transporting ATPase traps copper in enterocytes, preventing export to the bloodstream; tissues are therefore copper-deficient despite normal dietary intake

Clinical presentation:

Onset in male infants

Kinky/steely hair (pili torti) due to deficient lysyl oxidase (collagen/elastin crosslinking requires Cu)

Severe neurodegeneration

Seizures, hypotonia, and failure to thrive

Connective tissue abnormalities occur from impaired collagen crosslinking

Lab findings: ↓ serum copper, ↓ ceruloplasmin

Toxicity/Excess (Wilson Disease)

Autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism caused by mutations in ATP7B (chromosome 13q14.3), encoding a copper-transporting ATPase in hepatocytes. Loss of function impairs both biliary copper excretion and incorporation of copper into ceruloplasmin, leading to progressive copper accumulation in liver, brain, kidneys, and cornea.

Clinical presentation:

Onset typically in young adults (ages 5-35)

Hepatic manifestations (hepatitis, cirrhosis, acute liver failure) often precede neuropsychiatric features (eg, dysarthria, gait disturbance, asterixis [flapping tremor], personality changes)

Kayser-Fleischer rings (golden-brown deposits in the corneal periphery visible on slit-lamp examination) are pathognomonic when present but absent in ~50% of hepatic-only presentations

Lab findings:

↓ serum ceruloplasmin (< 20 mg/dL)

↑ 24-hour urinary copper (> 100 µg/day)

Elevated hepatic copper on liver biopsy (> 250 µg/g dry weight)

Serum total copper is often low because most circulating copper is ceruloplasmin-bound.

Treatment:

D-penicillamine: copper chelator, first-line

Trientine: chelator, for patients who cannot tolerate penicillamine

Zinc: inhibits intestinal copper absorption; used for maintenance or in asymptomatic patients

Selenium

Biochemistry & Function

Selenium is incorporated into selenoproteins as selenocysteine, the 21st amino acid. The most clinically relevant selenoproteins are glutathione peroxidase (reduces hydrogen peroxide and lipid peroxides, protecting against oxidative damage) and thioredoxin reductase. Selenium is also required for the enzyme iodothyronine deiodinase, which converts thyroxine (T4) to the active triiodothyronine (T3).

Deficiency

Keshan disease: a selenium-deficiency-associated dilated cardiomyopathy endemic to selenium-poor regions of China. Appears to be potentiated by concurrent coxsackievirus B infection.

Kashin-Beck disease: selenium-related osteoarthropathy causing joint degeneration in children; also endemic to selenium-poor regions of China.

Acquired selenium deficiency occurs with long-term total parenteral nutrition or severe malabsorption.

Toxicity

Selenosis from excessive intake: brittle nails and hair, garlic-like breath odor (from exhaled dimethylselenide), neurological symptoms, and GI upset

Iodine

Biochemistry & Function

Substrate for thyroid hormone synthesis

In the thyroid follicular cell, iodide (I-) is transported into the cell by the sodium-iodide symporter (NIS), oxidized by thyroperoxidase (TPO) in the presence of H2O2, and incorporated into thyroglobulin tyrosine residues (organification)

Produces monoiodotyrosine (MIT) and diiodotyrosine (DIT), which are coupled to form T3 and T4

Wolff-Chaikoff effect: transient inhibition of thyroid hormone synthesis that occurs after an acute iodine load; this is a protective autoregulatory mechanism

Jod-Basedow effect is the opposite of Wolff-Chaikoff effect: iodine loading in patients with underlying thyroid nodules (eg, multinodular goiter) can trigger hyperthyroidism by providing substrate for autonomous thyroid tissue

Deficiency

Goiter: thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)-driven thyroid hypertrophy in response to inadequate hormone production; the earliest sign of iodine deficiency

Hypothyroidism: fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, myxedema

Cretinism: congenital hypothyroidism from maternal iodine deficiency during pregnancy; characterized by intellectual disability, short stature, coarse facial features, macroglossia, umbilical hernia, and sensorineural deafness. Represents the most common preventable cause of intellectual disability worldwide

Iodine deficiency is prevented by iodized salt supplementation, standard in the United States since the 1920s. Deficiency remains prevalent in land-locked regions without access to seafood or iodized products

Toxicity

Chronic iodine excess can paradoxically cause hypothyroidism via sustained Wolff-Chaikoff blockade (failure of thyroid escape)

Amiodarone, a highly iodine-rich antiarrhythmic, is a common pharmacologic cause of both hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism (Jod-Basedow)

Fluoride

Biochemistry & Function

Incorporated into the hydroxyapatite mineral of tooth enamel and bone, forming fluorapatite, which is harder, less soluble, and more resistant to acid dissolution by oral bacteria than unmodified hydroxyapatite

Inhibits bacterial enolase, reducing lactic acid production that causes caries

Deficiency

Susceptibility to dental caries

Excess

Dental fluorosis (mild excess): white opacities or brown mottling of tooth enamel from excessive fluoride intake during enamel formation in childhood

Skeletal fluorosis (severe excess): joint pain, ligament calcification, and osteosclerosis from chronic high-dose exposure

Optimal fluoridation of public water reduces caries incidence without causing fluorosis.

Chromium

Biochemistry & Function

Trivalent chromium [Cr(III)] enhances insulin signaling by stabilizing the insulin-receptor complex via chromodulin, a chromium-binding oligopeptide that activates the insulin receptor's tyrosine kinase

Potentiates insulin-stimulated glucose uptake

Deficiency

Typically seen with prolonged total parenteral nutrition (TPN)

Impaired glucose tolerance

Insulin resistance

Toxicity

Hexavalent chromium [Cr(VI)] is a carcinogen (occupational exposure in welding, metal plating) associated with lung cancer and nasal septum perforation

Manganese

Biochemistry & Function

Metal cofactor for arginase in the urea cycle (ornithine → urea synthesis), mitochondrial superoxide dismutase (MnSOD), pyruvate carboxylase (gluconeogenesis), and glycosyltransferases (glycoprotein synthesis)

Deficiency

Dietary deficiency is rare

Toxicity

Occupational inhalation of manganese dust causes manganism: a parkinsonism-like syndrome with resting tremor, bradykinesia, rigidity, and psychiatric symptoms (manganese deposits preferentially in the basal ganglia)

Molybdenum

Biochemistry & Function

Metal cofactor for xanthine oxidase (catalyzes hypoxanthine → xanthine → uric acid, the final steps of purine catabolism), sulfite oxidase (converts sulfite to sulfate; deficiency causes accumulating sulfite toxicity with neurological damage), and aldehyde oxidase

Deficiency

Rare and occurs almost exclusively with prolonged TPN

Isolated sulfite oxidase deficiency (either molybdenum deficiency or genetic) causes severe neurological dysfunction, dislocated lenses, and accumulation of sulfite metabolites

Toxicity

High dietary molybdenum antagonizes copper absorption and can produce a gout-like syndrome (elevated uric acid) due to enhanced xanthine oxidase activity

Key Takeaways

Iron deficiency is the most common nutritional deficiency worldwide; produces microcytic, hypochromic anemia with ↓ ferritin, ↓ serum iron, ↑ TIBC, and ↓ transferrin saturation. Classic triad of severe deficiency: Plummer-Vinson syndrome (dysphagia + esophageal web + iron deficiency anemia).

Hereditary hemochromatosis: homozygous C282Y mutation in HFE → inappropriately low hepcidin → excess iron absorption. Classic triad: bronze diabetes (hyperpigmentation + diabetes mellitus), cirrhosis, and cardiomyopathy. Screen with transferrin saturation > 45%. Treat with therapeutic phlebotomy.

Zinc deficiency produces the classic triad: perioral/perineal dermatitis + diarrhea + alopecia (acrodermatitis enteropathica, AR, SLC39A4 mutation). Zinc also impairs wound healing, immune function (T-cell-mediated), and taste/smell.

Zinc toxicity: ↓ copper absorption → secondary copper deficiency (microcytic anemia + neurological findings). This mechanism is used therapeutically in Wilson disease.

Menkes disease (X-linked recessive, ATP7A): copper trapped in enterocytes → tissue copper deficiency → kinky/steely hair (pili torti), neurodegeneration, hypotonia. ↓ serum copper, ↓ ceruloplasmin. Onset in male infants.

Wilson disease (autosomal recessive, ATP7B, chromosome 13): copper accumulates in liver, brain, cornea → hepatitis/cirrhosis, neuropsychiatric dysfunction, Kayser-Fleischer rings, asterixis. ↓ ceruloplasmin, ↑ 24-hour urinary copper. Treat with D-penicillamine or trientine; use zinc for maintenance.

Selenium is required for glutathione peroxidase (antioxidant defense) and T4 → T3 conversion (iodothyronine deiodinase). Deficiency causes Keshan disease (dilated cardiomyopathy, endemic to selenium-poor regions of China).

Iodine is the substrate for T3/T4 synthesis. Deficiency → goiter, hypothyroidism, and cretinism (the most common preventable cause of intellectual disability worldwide). The Wolff-Chaikoff effect (acute iodine load → transient suppression of thyroid hormone synthesis) and the Jod-Basedow effect (iodine load → hyperthyroidism in autonomous nodular tissue) are both board-tested.

Fluoride: deficiency = dental caries; excess in childhood = dental fluorosis (white/brown mottling of tooth enamel)

Manganese: cofactor for arginase (urea cycle) and MnSOD; manganism = occupational parkinsonism

Molybdenum: cofactor for xanthine oxidase → purine catabolism → uric acid; sulfite oxidase deficiency → neurological damage

Teaching Cases

Case 1: Iron Deficiency Anemia

A 42-year-old woman with uterine fibroids presents with fatigue, koilonychia, ferritin 4 ng/mL, and TIBC 480 µg/dL. Peripheral smear shows hypochromic microcytic cells. Diagnosis: iron deficiency anemia from chronic blood loss; treat with oral ferrous sulfate. Key teaching: ferritin is the most sensitive early marker; TIBC rises in deficiency, distinguishing it from anemia of chronic disease.

Case 2: Hereditary Hemochromatosis

A 52-year-old man of Northern European descent presents with bronze skin, MCP arthralgias, and fasting glucose 210 mg/dL. Transferrin saturation is 62%; HFE testing confirms C282Y homozygosity. Diagnosis: hereditary hemochromatosis; treat with therapeutic phlebotomy. Key teaching: transferrin saturation > 45% is the most sensitive screening test; MCP arthropathy responds poorly to phlebotomy.

Case 3: Wilson Disease

A 19-year-old man presents with dysarthria, asterixis, and golden-brown corneal rings on slit-lamp. Ceruloplasmin is 8 mg/dL and 24-hour urine copper is 280 µg/day. Diagnosis: Wilson disease; treat with D-penicillamine or trientine. Key teaching: Kayser-Fleischer rings are absent in ~50% of hepatic-only presentations; ceruloplasmin is low because copper is not incorporated into it normally.

Case 4: Acrodermatitis Enteropathica

A 9-month-old boy develops periorificial dermatitis, diarrhea, and alopecia three weeks after weaning from breast milk. Serum zinc is low; SLC39A4 mutation confirmed. Diagnosis: acrodermatitis enteropathica; breast milk picolinic acid masks the absorptive defect until weaning. Key teaching: the triad plus onset at weaning is pathognomonic; oral zinc is curative.
